Dear Corvale Mobility Hiring Team,

I’m applying for the Cloud Infrastructure / DevOps Contractor – Fleet Connectivity role. Over the past seven years in QA automation, I’ve increasingly focused on the infrastructure that helps development teams build, test and release reliably. At Odrava Health Software, I own GitLab CI pipelines for three product teams and have built ephemeral test environments using Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster.

I’ve improved pipeline duration from 38 to 14 minutes, reducing monthly CI runner costs by about 30%, and built merge-request environments with the application, PostgreSQL and seeded data that are removed automatically after merge or inactivity. This work has involved making infrastructure practical for teams to use and supporting feature reviews and end-to-end testing before merge. I’ve also written the internal “How Our CI Works” guide used in onboarding and mentored two QA interns.

Alongside my work, I built a three-node k3s homelab where applications are deployed from Git using Argo CD, with Prometheus, Grafana and Loki for monitoring. I’ve also provisioned a small Hetzner VPS with Terraform. These projects have helped me develop hands-on experience with infrastructure automation and observability, while my professional work has given me a strong foundation in Linux, CI/CD and supporting reliable software delivery.

Corvale’s plans to connect a new train fleet to its cloud platform make this an especially interesting infrastructure challenge. I’d welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience building test infrastructure and improving delivery workflows could contribute to the Fleet Connectivity team.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Marta Kowal-Brandt

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is clear, professional, concise, and well structured. It uses credible quantified achievements—pipeline time reduced from 38 to 14 minutes and runner costs reduced by approximately 30%—and explains the relevance of the candidate’s CI/CD, Kubernetes, observability, and Terraform experience. The progression from professional work to the personal k3s project is logical. The main weakness is that it presents a relatively general fit for a demanding infrastructure role and does not make several relevant, truthful details explicit, particularly TLS/certificate management, AWS fundamentals, and the candidate’s experience communicating technical practices across teams.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter is highly parseable: it uses standard paragraphs, no tables or graphics, and includes useful terms such as DevOps, CI/CD, GitLab CI, Helm, Kubernetes, Docker, PostgreSQL, k3s, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Terraform, Linux, and infrastructure automation. However, ATS and AI screening alignment would improve if the letter used additional supported terms from the advertisement, including AWS, TLS, certificate management, stakeholder collaboration, and technical documentation. It should not add Terragrunt, mTLS, production cloud operation, or broader security claims because the candidate information does not support them. AI screening probability is moderate to good for CI/CD and test-infrastructure keywords, but weaker for the role’s core cloud infrastructure, networking, and systems-design requirements.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The letter demonstrates a credible adjacent fit: hands-on ownership of CI/CD, ephemeral Kubernetes test environments, Helm, observability, infrastructure automation, analytical pipeline optimisation, and technical documentation. It also supports the company’s engineering-led and ownership-oriented culture through examples of owning delivery workflows, improving team practices, and enabling product teams to review changes. The role is nevertheless a stretch because the candidate does not have strong Terraform and Terragrunt experience, mTLS or broader network-design experience, demonstrated production AWS infrastructure operation, IoT/automotive or remote-device integration, or virtual-machine experience. These are candidate-background gaps rather than defects that can be solved through wording. The letter should make the strongest adjacent evidence more explicit without overstating seniority or scope.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL ISSUES: None identified; the cover letter does not contain a clear hallucination when cross-referenced with the original candidate information.

MINOR, HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENTS:
1. In the paragraph beginning “Alongside my work,” add the supported TLS and certificate-management detail after the sentence about Prometheus, Grafana and Loki. For example: “The homelab also uses Traefik ingress with cert-manager-managed TLS certificates.” This adds a truthful networking/security keyword without claiming unsupported mTLS expertise.
2. In the same paragraph, add the candidate’s truthful AWS exposure after the Terraform sentence: “I also have basic personal learning experience with AWS EC2 and S3.” Do not describe this as production AWS operation or as advanced AWS expertise.
3. In the second paragraph, make stakeholder collaboration more explicit by revising “This work has involved making infrastructure practical for teams to use and supporting feature reviews...” to: “This work required coordinating practical workflows for three product teams and enabled QA and product stakeholders to review features before merge.” This is supported by the candidate’s ownership of pipelines for three teams and the merge-request environments used by QA and product teams.
4. In the final paragraph, strengthen the communication and technical-leadership evidence by adding the internal documentation example: “I also authored the internal ‘How Our CI Works’ guide, now used in onboarding, which reflects my focus on making technical systems understandable and approachable for other teams.”
5. In the opening paragraph, replace the broad phrase “strong foundation in Linux, CI/CD and supporting reliable software delivery” with the more specific supported wording: “hands-on experience with Linux-based CI/CD workflows, GitLab CI ownership, Helm-deployed Kubernetes test environments, and reliable software delivery.” This improves keyword precision while avoiding an unsupported claim of full production platform ownership.
6. Do not add “Terragrunt,” “mTLS,” IoT/automotive integration, production AWS infrastructure, on-call ownership, or claims of operating the Kubernetes cluster itself. The candidate information supports Terraform on a personal Hetzner project, TLS through cert-manager in the homelab, and namespace-level Kubernetes work rather than those broader claims.

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is professional, readable, and supported by quantified achievements. It clearly explains the candidate’s transition from QA automation toward DevOps/platform infrastructure and uses relevant evidence: CI/CD ownership, Kubernetes test environments, Terraform, GitOps, observability, and pipeline optimisation. The strongest section is the second paragraph, which connects specific actions to measurable results. However, the letter is somewhat repetitive: the Odrava CI guide, onboarding use, and mentoring are mentioned more than once, and the third paragraph repeats several technologies and claims already made earlier. The opening is also fairly broad for a role involving cloud infrastructure, system design, networking, and fleet connectivity. The letter does not clearly distinguish professional infrastructure experience from personal-project experience until fairly late, although it generally remains truthful and transparent.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter is ATS-readable: it uses conventional paragraphs, standard text, no problematic tables or graphics, and includes several relevant terms such as GitLab CI, Helm, Kubernetes, Docker, PostgreSQL, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Terraform, AWS EC2, AWS S3, infrastructure automation, observability, and CI/CD. AI screening probability is moderate rather than high because several central terms from the advertisement are absent or only indirectly addressed, especially Terragrunt, systems architecture/system design, networking, mutual TLS (mTLS), security awareness, and cloud environment operation. These are genuine experience gaps in the supplied candidate information, so they should not be inserted into the letter as claims. The document could also use the exact phrase “infrastructure as code” where supported by the Terraform work and make the AWS scope more concise and clearly labelled as basic personal learning.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The letter aligns well with the role’s DevOps/platform-infrastructure direction, particularly through ownership of CI/CD for three teams, ephemeral Kubernetes environments, infrastructure automation, observability, analytical pipeline improvements, documentation, and stakeholder enablement. It also reflects relevant cultural signals such as ownership, collaboration, and making technical systems approachable. The strongest quantified evidence is the reduction from 38 to 14 minutes and the approximately 30% reduction in runner costs. The candidate has a partial match for hands-on infrastructure engineering: professional work involves test infrastructure and namespace-level Kubernetes access, while Terraform, k3s, and GitOps are personal projects. The supplied material shows gaps in strong Terraform and Terragrunt experience, systems architecture and system design, mTLS/network design, practical security beyond TLS configuration, IoT or remote-device integration, backend/full-stack development, and virtual-machine experience. AWS is shown only at basic personal-learning level. These are candidate-profile gaps rather than defects that can be solved through rewriting.
critique.improvement_instructions:
MINOR, HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENTS ONLY:
1. In the opening paragraph, make the role alignment more specific and reduce the generic transition wording. Replace “I’ve increasingly focused on the infrastructure that helps development teams build, test and release reliably” with “For the past two-plus years, I have owned CI/CD and test-infrastructure work for three product teams, including GitLab CI pipelines and Helm-deployed Kubernetes environments.” This preserves the truthful scope and foregrounds the most relevant evidence immediately.

2. In the second paragraph, remove the repeated reference to the internal guide and mentoring. Keep the existing sentence “I’ve also written the internal ‘How Our CI Works’ guide used in onboarding and mentored two QA interns,” but delete the later sentence beginning “I also authored the internal ‘How Our CI Works’ guide...” in the fourth paragraph. Use the final paragraph for company and role motivation instead.

3. In the third paragraph, make the professional-versus-personal scope explicit and add the supported ATS phrase “infrastructure as code.” For example, change “I’ve also provisioned a small Hetzner VPS with Terraform” to “In a personal project, I provisioned infrastructure for a small Hetzner VPS with Terraform, giving me hands-on practice with infrastructure as code.” Retain “personal project” so the letter does not imply production Terraform ownership.

4. In the third paragraph, replace the broad phrase “hands-on experience with Linux-based CI/CD workflows” with the more concrete, supportable wording “hands-on experience with Linux, GitLab CI, Helm, Docker, and Kubernetes test environments.” If desired, add “with namespace-level access on the shared Kubernetes cluster” to make the operational scope precise and avoid implying cluster administration.

5. In the final paragraph, connect the candidate’s documented strengths to the company’s stated ownership and collaboration culture without claiming fleet, IoT, or train-to-cloud experience. For example, replace “could contribute to the Fleet Connectivity team” with “could contribute to the Fleet Connectivity team through reliable delivery workflows, observable test infrastructure, clear technical documentation, and collaborative work with development and QA stakeholders.”

In the opening paragraph, change “the infrastructure that helps development teams build, test and release reliably” to “the CI/CD and test infrastructure that helps development teams build, test and release reliably.” This uses more precise terminology already supported by the candidate’s experience and improves ATS matching for the demonstrated area.

Dear Corvale Mobility Hiring Team,

I’m applying for the Cloud Infrastructure / DevOps Contractor – Fleet Connectivity role. Over seven years in QA automation, I’ve focused on CI/CD and test infrastructure helping teams build, test and release reliably.

At Odrava Health Software, I own GitLab CI pipelines and test infrastructure for three product teams. I’ve improved pipeline duration from 38 to 14 minutes, reducing monthly CI runner costs by about 30%. I built per-merge-request ephemeral test environments using Docker Compose and Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster, including PostgreSQL and seeded data, so QA and product teams could review changes before merge.

Alongside my work, I built a three-node k3s homelab using Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Traefik and cert-manager, and provisioned a Hetzner VPS with Terraform.

I authored the internal ‘How Our CI Works’ guide used in onboarding and built Python/PostgreSQL tooling and Grafana dashboards that helped teams identify and reduce flaky tests.

Corvale’s planned train fleet makes this an interesting infrastructure challenge. I would welcome discussing how I could contribute to CI/CD, observable delivery workflows, Kubernetes-based environments and infrastructure automation while growing toward broader cloud platform ownership.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Marta Kowal-Brandt
